newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - Berlin vulnerable to Allied bombs 52 years after war.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Berlin vulnerable to Allied bombs 52 years after war.

text.p: The threat from Allied bombing raids is still far from over in Germany, even though the war ended 52 years ago.
The risk comes from unexploded bombs lying just below the ground where they fell.

Nearly every week, a neighbourhood in or around Berlin receives a phone call from the police telling inhabitants to evacuate their homes until a World War Two bomb is defused and they are out of danger.

"Here we are, seven to eight years before retirement, but the work could last at least another generation," said Norbert Funke, the greying director of Berlin Aerial Photography Analysis, which examines U.S. and British wartime photographs for signs of unexploded bombs beneath the city.

Funke and his four colleagues spend six hours a day squinting over the black-and-white stereoscopic (three-dimensional) pictures, looking for shallow craters where bombs during the 1940s may have landed but not exploded.

Once they find the small crescent path of an undetonated bomb on one of their 8,000 photos, which British and U.S. air forces took to determine a raid's success, they send surveying teams with metal detectors to investigate on site.
NIGHTMARE CAME TRUE

In 1983 a 500 kg (1,100 lb) bomb went off in front of a school in a central Berlin district, fortunately during the summer holiday. Later that year, the city of West Berlin opened Funke's office and entrusted his team with preventing a repeat.

Despite 14 years of work, the team -- which now covers the whole of the Berlin area -- cannot say a district is completely free of danger. Explosives continually surface under schools, behind the Brandenburg Gate, in the future federal government quarter.

"If you worked eight hours a day at this, a normal work day for most people, you wouldn't make it," Funke said, referring to of the level of concentration required. "The biggest worry is that you'll overlook something."

In September 1994, Funke's nightmare came true. Three construction workers were killed and several injured when an excavator tripped the fuse of a U.S. bomb which had been covered by only a few metres (feet) of dirt.
Officials from the Berlin prosecutors' office questioned Funke's staff shortly after the blast. Although they were cleared of any negligence, Funke said the incident still haunted him.
"You ask yourself who should take the blame," he said. "That is always an issue for us."
Since that explosion, construction teams are required to consult the department's aerial photograph analyses before beginning work.
MOST BOMBED GERMAN CITY
As the capital of Nazi Germany, more bombs fell on Berlin duirng 1943 and 1944 than any other German city. Up to 50,000 died in the raids.

"Every day, Allied planes swooped by once or twice. In a big attack, you saw 1,200 fighter planes. The skies were black," Funke said. "Of course, during that time, bombs were also defused, but just after 1945, you had your own life to worry about."
Funke estimates between 10 and 20 percent of those bombs did not go off.

Although countries such as Afghanistan, Angola, Cambodia, Laos and former Yugoslavia also suffer from this typical aftermath of war, Berlin and its metropolitan area is perhaps the most densely-populated region still afflicted.

Hans-Juergen Gembus, director of the Berlin ammunition removal department, said every year his office locates 25 unexploded bombs and up to 6,000 grenades, which prove more difficult to find because of their size.
In February, five young children were injured, some seriously, when they discovered a German Wehrmacht hand grenade in the courtyard of their apartment block.
STEADY NERVES NEEDED

Gembus and his co-workers investigate sites that Funke's office identifies as at risk. When they find a bomb using metal detectors, they hand the job to explosives experts at the local police department.
They try to defuse the old and often rusted bombs on site but if that is not possible, they take them to an isolated site in Grunewald, a Berlin forest, and detonate them there.
Thousands in the densely-populated town of Oranienburg, north of Berlin, have been evacuated 46 times since German unification in 1990, to prevent casualities in case the work goes wrong.

Oranienburg was nearly levelled by the Allies during the war because of its contributions to Adolf Hitler's atomic bomb project. Scientists there had already succeeded in creating "heavy water", one of the weapon's key components.

Bombs buried across eastern Germany have posed a particular danger since unification because of the increase in building work there and decades of neglect by the East German government when it came to cleaning up after the war.

"When the East Germans found the bombs, they would remove them," Funke said. "But they didn't do what we do, and that is seek them out before someone comes upon them...From this point of view, 1990 was a new beginning for us."

He estimated that 90 percent of his office's work is concentrated in east Berlin, but their task is not immune to hard times in the cash-strapped region. As Germany attempts to tighten its belt, even bomb disposal is a threatened industry.

Berlin budgeted 10 million marks ($5.9 million) this year for bomb disposal work, down by a third since the late 1980s. Officials fear further cost-cutting will make it even harder for them, until a catastrophe reignites the political will. ($ = 1.681 German Marks)
